_sources.usda: USDA FoodData Central, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (record named in each entry), read 2026-10-27
_sources.nihOds: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets (Iron, Folate, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, Magnesium, Zinc, Potassium, Vitamin A, Calcium, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Vitamin E), https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/; reference intakes as listed in build_draft_batch.py (RDA for adult women)

beef.desc: Beef, ground, 90% lean meat / 10% fat, patty, cooked, pan-broiled
beef.offers: Cooked 90% lean ground beef is a dense source of vitamin B12 (about 99% of the reference in 3 ounces), zinc (about 67%) and iron (about 13%), with about 21 g of protein.
beef.how: Brown for sauces, chilli and tacos, shape into burgers, or mix with grated vegetables or lentils to stretch it. Pair with vitamin C foods such as tomatoes or peppers.
beef.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Iron from meat is absorbed more readily than iron from plant foods, so beef is an efficient source; 3 ounces provide about 2.4 mg.
beef.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
beef.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "beef" is generic. The record is 90% lean ground beef, cooked; steaks, roasts and fattier mince differ.
beef.name: Beef

tempeh.state: as sold (fermented soybean cake), not cooked
tempeh.offers: Tempeh is a firm, nutty cake of fermented whole soybeans. Half a cup gives about 17 g of protein, magnesium (about 22% of the reference), potassium and iron.
tempeh.how: Slice or crumble and pan-fry, bake or grill with a marinade, or simmer into curries and chilli. Steaming it for a few minutes first mellows its flavour.
tempeh.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Tempeh adds plant iron (about 2.2 mg in this serving), which is absorbed less readily than iron from meat; vitamin C in the same meal helps.
tempeh.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
tempeh.name: Tempeh

chicken.desc: Chicken, broilers or fryers, breast, meat only, cooked, roasted
chicken.portion: ½ breast, skinless (USDA: 0.5 breast, bone and skin removed = 86 g)
chicken.offers: Roasted skinless chicken breast is a lean, high-protein food: half a breast gives about 27 g of protein for about 142 calories, plus vitamin B12 and zinc.
chicken.how: Roast, grill, poach or pan-fry, then slice into salads and wraps, shred into soups and bowls, or serve with vegetables and grains.
chicken.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for chicken; it is mainly a lean protein source.
chicken.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
chicken.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "chicken" is generic; the record is skinless breast. Thighs and skin-on cuts have more fat and more iron and zinc.
chicken.name: Chicken

eggs.offers: A hard-boiled egg gives about 6 g of protein, vitamin B12, vitamin A and some vitamin D for about 78 calories.
eggs.how: Boil, poach, scramble or bake; slice into salads, grain bowls and sandwiches. Cook until the white and yolk are firm.
eggs.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for eggs. A single egg supplies a modest share of most nutrients, and one of the few foods with some vitamin D.
eggs.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
eggs.name: Eggs

tofu.desc: Tofu, raw, firm, prepared with calcium sulfate
tofu.state: raw (as sold), firm, set with calcium sulfate
tofu.offers: Firm tofu set with calcium sulfate is a plant protein with a lot of calcium: a quarter block gives about 14 g of protein and about 55% of the calcium reference, plus zinc and magnesium.
tofu.how: Press and cube for stir-fries and curries, crumble into scrambles, bake or pan-fry until golden, or blend silken types into sauces. It takes on the flavour of what it is cooked with.
tofu.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). Tofu made with calcium sulfate is one of the richer non-dairy sources; check the label, as tofu set with other coagulants has much less.
tofu.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
tofu.reviewNote: Calcium depends on the coagulant: tofu set with calcium sulfate is high in calcium, tofu set with nigari (magnesium chloride) is not. The record is the calcium-sulfate type.
tofu.name: Tofu

pork.desc: Pork, fresh, loin, whole, separable lean only, cooked, roasted
pork.offers: Roasted lean pork loin gives about 24 g of protein, zinc (about 27% of the reference), vitamin B12 and potassium in 3 ounces, for about 178 calories.
pork.how: Roast, grill or pan-sear, then slice thinly; it works with fruit, mustard and herbs, in stir-fries, or shredded into tacos.
pork.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Lean loin is a modest source of iron (about 0.9 mg in this serving); other cuts and organ meats differ.
pork.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pork.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "pork" is generic; the record is roasted lean loin. Other cuts, and processed pork, differ.
pork.name: Pork

lamb.desc: Lamb, leg, shank half, separable lean only, trimmed to 1/4" fat, choice, cooked, roasted
lamb.offers: Roasted lean leg of lamb is a dense source of vitamin B12 (about 96% of the reference in 3 ounces), zinc (about 53%) and protein (about 24 g).
lamb.how: Roast with garlic, rosemary and lemon, grill slices, or braise in stews and curries; rest the meat before carving.
lamb.cycle: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Lamb provides iron from meat (about 1.8 mg in this serving), absorbed more readily than iron from plants.
lamb.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
lamb.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "lamb" is generic; the record is roasted lean leg (shank half). Other cuts differ.
lamb.name: Lamb

turkey.desc: Turkey, whole, breast, meat only, cooked, roasted
turkey.offers: Roasted turkey breast is a very lean, high-protein meat: 3 ounces give about 26 g of protein for 125 calories, plus zinc and a little vitamin B12.
turkey.how: Roast and slice for sandwiches and salads, shred into soups, or use in stir-fries and bowls.
turkey.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for turkey; it is mainly a lean protein source.
turkey.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
turkey.reviewNote: Roasted breast, meat only; dark meat and deli turkey differ.
turkey.name: Turkey

feta.offers: Feta is a brined, tangy white cheese. An ounce gives calcium (about 14% of the reference), vitamin B12 and zinc for about 75 calories. It is salty.
feta.how: Crumble over salads, roasted vegetables and eggs, bake with tomatoes, or serve with olives and bread.
feta.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). An ounce of feta supplies about 140 mg, about 14% of that.
feta.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
feta.name: Feta

plain-yogurt.offers: A 6-ounce container of plain whole-milk yogurt gives calcium (about 21% of the reference), vitamin B12, zinc and about 6 g of protein.
plain-yogurt.how: Eat with fruit, nuts and seeds, stir into soups and curries, blend into smoothies and dressings, or use in baking in place of cream.
plain-yogurt.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). A container of plain yogurt supplies about 206 mg, about 21% of that. No phase-specific claim is made.
plain-yogurt.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
plain-yogurt.reviewNote: Whole-milk plain yogurt; low-fat and fat-free versions have similar protein and calcium with less fat. Vitamin D is only present if the milk is fortified.
plain-yogurt.name: Plain yogurt

cottage-cheese.offers: Half a cup of low-fat cottage cheese gives about 12 g of protein, vitamin B12 and calcium (about 13% of the reference) for only 92 calories.
cottage-cheese.how: Eat with fruit or tomatoes, spread on toast, blend into pancake batter and dips, or layer into lasagne.
cottage-cheese.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for cottage cheese; it is mainly a high-protein, lower-fat dairy food.
cottage-cheese.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
cottage-cheese.name: Cottage cheese

kefir.state: low-fat plain kefir (a branded USDA record)
kefir.offers: A cup of low-fat plain kefir, a tangy drinkable fermented milk, gives calcium (about 32% of the reference), vitamin A, vitamin B12 and about 9 g of protein for 104 calories.
kefir.how: Drink cold on its own, blend into smoothies, pour over cereal or fruit, or use in place of buttermilk in baking and dressings.
kefir.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). A cup of kefir supplies about 316 mg, about 32% of that. No phase-specific claim is made for kefir.
kefir.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
kefir.reviewNote: The only USDA kefir records are branded (Lifeway); values for other kefirs differ, and live-culture content is not in a nutrient record.
kefir.name: Kefir

ricotta.offers: Half a cup of whole-milk ricotta, a soft, mild fresh cheese, gives calcium (about 26% of the reference), vitamin A and vitamin B12 with about 9 g of protein.
ricotta.how: Spread on toast with honey or fruit, fold into pasta and lasagne, or mix into pancakes and baking.
ricotta.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). Half a cup supplies about 255 mg, about 26% of that.
ricotta.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
ricotta.name: Ricotta

goat-cheese.offers: An ounce of soft goat cheese gives about 5 g of protein and vitamin A (about 12% of the reference), with some calcium and iron, for about 75 calories.
goat-cheese.how: Crumble over salads and roasted vegetables, spread on toast, or bake until warm and soft.
goat-cheese.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for goat cheese.
goat-cheese.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
goat-cheese.name: Goat cheese

greek-yogurt.portion: 1 container, 6 ounces (170 g; USDA lists no household measure for this record)
greek-yogurt.offers: A 6-ounce container of plain whole-milk Greek yogurt gives about 15 g of protein, vitamin B12 (about 53% of the reference) and calcium (about 17%).
greek-yogurt.how: Eat with fruit and honey, use in dips and dressings such as tzatziki, or in place of cream or sour cream.
greek-yogurt.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). A container supplies about 170 mg, about 17% of that. No phase-specific claim is made.
greek-yogurt.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
greek-yogurt.reviewNote: USDA lists no household measure for this record; 170 g (a 6-ounce container) is my choice, not USDA's. The catalogue entry is generic: fat-free Greek yogurt has less fat and similar protein.
greek-yogurt.name: Greek yogurt

mozzarella.offers: An ounce of whole-milk mozzarella gives about 6 g of protein, calcium (about 14% of the reference) and vitamin B12 for about 85 calories.
mozzarella.how: Melt on pizza and baked pasta, tear fresh mozzarella over tomatoes and basil, or add to sandwiches and salads.
mozzarella.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). An ounce supplies about 143 mg, about 14% of that.
mozzarella.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
mozzarella.name: Mozzarella

swiss-cheese.offers: A slice of Swiss cheese gives calcium (about 25% of the reference), vitamin B12 and zinc, with about 7.6 g of protein for about 110 calories.
swiss-cheese.how: Melt into sandwiches, quiche and gratins, or slice with fruit and bread.
swiss-cheese.cycle: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). A slice supplies about 249 mg, about 25% of that.
swiss-cheese.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
swiss-cheese.name: Swiss cheese

miso.offers: Miso is a salty, savoury fermented soybean paste. A tablespoon gives protein, fibre and a little zinc and iron for about 34 calories, mainly as flavour.
miso.how: Whisk into hot (not boiling) water for soup, stir into dressings and marinades, or glaze vegetables and fish. A little goes a long way.
miso.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for miso. It is used in small amounts and is high in sodium (see the caution).
miso.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
miso.reviewNote: Miso is very high in sodium (existing catalogue caution: high in salt). Sodium is not in the key list and no sourced salt caution has been added.
miso.name: Miso

sauerkraut.offers: Canned sauerkraut is salty, tangy fermented cabbage with vitamin C (about 14% of the reference in half a cup), some iron and fibre, for only about 13 calories.
sauerkraut.how: Serve alongside sausages and roast meats, pile onto sandwiches, or add to salads and grain bowls. Drain or rinse to reduce the salt.
sauerkraut.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for sauerkraut. This record is canned and pasteurised; raw sauerkraut differs.
sauerkraut.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
sauerkraut.reviewNote: Canned sauerkraut is pasteurised; raw, refrigerated sauerkraut keeps live cultures, which a nutrient record does not capture. It is high in sodium (existing caution).
sauerkraut.name: Sauerkraut

pickles.desc: Pickles, cucumber, dill or kosher dill
pickles.offers: A dill pickle spear is a very low-energy, salty condiment with little else nutritionally: a small spear is about 4 calories.
pickles.how: Eat with sandwiches and burgers, chop into dressings and tartare sauce, or serve with cheese and cold meats.
pickles.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for pickles. They are high in sodium (see the caution).
pickles.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pickles.reviewNote: Vinegar pickles are not live-fermented; fermented pickles differ. Very high in sodium (existing caution), not shown.
pickles.name: Pickles

kimchi.offers: Kimchi is spicy fermented cabbage. Half a cup gives folate and iron (about 10% each), vitamin K and a little fibre for only about 11 calories.
kimchi.how: Eat as a side, stir into fried rice, noodles and soups, or add to eggs and sandwiches.
kimchi.cycle: No cycle-phase claim is made for kimchi. It is high in sodium, and many kimchis contain fish sauce (see the caution).
kimchi.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
kimchi.reviewNote: Kimchi recipes vary (fish sauce, salt, chilli); the record is a USDA average. It is high in sodium; no caution is recorded in the catalogue.
kimchi.name: Kimchi
